k6.title: Gustar, reflexive verbs and object pronouns

k1-intro.text: Spanish has two verbs for “to be”: *ser* and *estar*. You need them to say who you are, where you are from, where you are and how you feel. Almost every first conversation uses them.

k1-why.text: English has one verb here and Spanish has two, so you make this choice all the time. It can even change the meaning: *Es aburrido* = he is boring. *Está aburrido* = he is bored.
k1-why.title: Why is this so important?

k1-h1.text: Subject pronouns and the two verbs

k1-rule1.text: The verb ending already shows the person, so Spanish often drops the pronoun: *Soy Pablo. Estoy en Bilbao.* Use the pronoun for contrast or to be clear: *Yo soy de Vigo y ella es de Cádiz.* There is no pronoun for “it”: *Es grande.*

k1-m1.text: *Tú* is for friends, family, children and people your age. In Spain people use it a lot, also at work. *Usted* shows respect: if you are not sure at an office, start with it. It takes the same verb form as *él* and *ella*: *¿Usted es la doctora?* In Latin America people say *ustedes* instead of *vosotros*, also with friends.

k1-h2.text: ser: who or what someone or something is

head: Use
Example
cells: what someone or something is like

k1-m2.text: A job needs no article after *ser*: *Soy enfermera*, not *Soy una enfermera*. Your age goes with *tener*, not *ser*: *Tengo 31 años.*

k1-err.text: For the place of a person or a thing, use *estar*, never *ser*.

k2-intro.text: We use the present tense for habits and facts, for what is happening now, and often for the near future: *Vivo en Sevilla. Carmen trabaja de noche. Mañana trabajo por la tarde.*

k2-rule1.text: Every Spanish verb ends in *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* in the dictionary. Take off this ending and add the ending for the person.

k2-m1.text: The *-er* and *-ir* endings are the same, except with *nosotros* and *vosotros*: *comemos / vivimos*, *coméis / vivís*. The *vosotros* forms have a written accent. Stress is usually on the last syllable but one: *HA-blo, VI-ves*.

k2-h3.text: How often? Words that often go with the present

k2-m2.text: *Los lunes* means every Monday: *Los lunes trabajo en casa.* *El lunes* means this coming Monday: *El lunes tengo cita.* Spanish uses no word for “on” here.

k2-err.text: The form with *-ar*, *-er* or *-ir* is only the dictionary form. In a sentence, the verb needs the ending for the person, and you usually don't need *yo*.

k3-intro.text: Spanish needs no helping verb like “do” in questions and negatives. A question starts with ¿ and ends with ?, and your voice goes up. A negative usually needs only the word *no*.

k3-why.text: Asking is how you get things done: at the town hall, at the doctor's, at the bank. With a few question words and *no*, you can ask for what you need and say what is not the case.
k3-why.title: Why is this so important?

k3-rule1.text: Take a normal sentence, write ¿ … ? around it and let your voice rise. The words don't have to change. The subject can also go after the verb: *¿Trabaja Lucía hoy?*

k3-rule2.text: Question words always have a written accent. After the question word comes the verb, then the subject: *¿Dónde vive Javier?* (not *¿Dónde Javier vive?*). A preposition goes before the question word, never at the end: *¿De dónde eres? ¿Con quién vives?*
k3-rule2.title: Question word + verb + subject

head: Question word
Asks about
Example
cells: the way, what it is like
a price, an amount, a number

k3-m1.text: *¿Por qué?* asks why: two words with an accent. *Porque* answers: one word, no accent. *¿Por qué estudias español? Porque vivo aquí.* *Cuánto* agrees with its noun: *¿Cuántos años tienes? ¿Cuánta leche quieres?*

k3-rule3.text: Put *no* right before the verb. In a short answer you often hear it twice: the first *no* answers, the second makes the verb negative: *¿Trabajas hoy? No, no trabajo.*

k3-rule4.text: After the verb, Spanish uses a second negative word: *No tengo nada.* If the negative word comes before the verb, *no* goes away: *Nunca como carne. Nadie sabe.*

k3-err.text: In English, two negatives cancel each other out. In Spanish they don't: with *no* before the verb, use *nada*, *nadie* or *nunca*.

k4-intro.text: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, also words for things. Articles and adjectives change to match the noun: *el piso pequeño, la casa pequeña, los pisos pequeños, las casas pequeñas*.

k4-rule1.text: The ending of a noun usually tells you. For other endings, learn the word together with its article.

k4-m1.text: Common exceptions: *el día, el problema, el idioma, el mapa* are masculine; *la mano, la foto, la moto* are feminine. Feminine nouns with a stressed *a-* at the start take *el* in the singular: *el agua fría* (but *las aguas*).

k4-rule2.text: Spanish uses *el, la, los, las* also for things in general, where English has no article: *Me gusta el café. Los niños juegan mucho.* It uses no *un* or *una* for jobs after *ser*, or for things people normally have one of: *Es médica. Tengo coche.*

k4-m2.text: *a* + *el* = *al*, and *de* + *el* = *del*: *Voy al médico. Vengo del trabajo.* Not with *la*: *Voy a la farmacia.*

head: Rule
Singular → plural
cells: the written accent can go or come

k4-rule3.text: An adjective usually goes after the noun and agrees with it. For a mixed group of men and women, use the masculine plural: *Mis hijos son altos* can mean sons and daughters.

k4-rule4.text: *Hay* means “there is” and “there are”, and it has only this one form. Use it for new information, with *un, una*, a number or no article. For a known, particular thing, use *está* or *están*.

k4-err.text: *Coche* is masculine, so the article and the adjective are masculine too. A noun in *-e* doesn't show its gender: learn it with the article.

k5-intro.text: The most common Spanish verbs are irregular. The good news: there are only a few patterns, and the endings stay almost the same as in Chapter 2.

k5-m1.text: *Tener* is for age, hunger and more, where English uses “be”: *Tengo 31 años. Tengo hambre. Tengo frío.* *Ir* goes with *a*: *Voy a Madrid. Vamos al médico.*

k5-h2.text: Irregular only in the yo form

k5-rule1.text: Some verbs are irregular only with *yo*. All the other persons are regular.

k5-m2.text: *Saber* is to know a fact or how to do something: *Sé conducir.* *Conocer* is to know a person or a place: *Conozco Sevilla. Conozco a Lucía.* A person needs *a* after the verb.

k5-rule2.text: In these verbs a vowel in the stem changes in every form except *nosotros* and *vosotros*. The endings are normal.

k5-err.text: *Saber* is irregular with *yo*: *sé*. Learn the *yo* form together with the verb: *sé, hago, tengo, salgo*.

k6-intro.text: Spanish has small pronouns (*me, te, lo, la, le, se…*) that usually go right before the verb. This chapter shows the three patterns you use every day.

k6-rule1.text: With *gustar*, the thing you like is the subject: *Me gusta el café* means “coffee pleases me”. So the verb agrees with the thing: *gusta* for one thing or a verb, *gustan* for more than one thing. The words *a mí, a ti…* are extra, for emphasis or contrast.

k6-m1.text: To agree: *Me gusta el café. A mí también.* / *No me gusta el café. A mí tampoco.* Verbs like *encantar* and *doler* work the same way: *Me encantan las tapas. Me duele la cabeza.*

k6-rule2.text: These verbs have *se* at the end in the dictionary: *levantarse*. The pronoun changes with the person and goes before the verb. Many of them describe your daily routine.

k6-m2.text: With an infinitive, the pronoun can go on the end of it or before the first verb. Both are right: *Quiero ducharme. Me quiero duchar.*

k6-rule3.text: An object pronoun replaces a person or a thing. A direct object answers “what?” or “who?”. An indirect object answers “to whom?”. Only the third person has different forms.

k6-m3.text: A person as direct object takes *a*: *Veo a Ana.* (a thing doesn't: *Veo la casa*). With two pronouns, the indirect one comes first, and *le* or *les* becomes *se*: *Se lo doy.* In Spain you may also hear *Le veo* for a man; *Lo veo* is always right.

k6-err.text: With more than one thing, use *gustan*. The verb agrees with what you like, not with the person.

k7-intro.text: Many everyday meanings come from two verbs together. Only the first verb changes; the second stays an infinitive or a gerund.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
cells: have to: you or someone in particular
you have to: a rule for everybody

k7-rule1.text: The first verb takes the ending for the person; the infinitive never changes. *Hay que* has only this one form.

k7-m1.text: *No tienes que venir* = it isn't necessary. *No debes venir* = you shouldn't come. *No puedes venir* = you can't, or you aren't allowed. And *Sé conducir* = I know how; *Hoy no puedo conducir* = today I can't.

k7-h2.text: ir a + infinitive: the near future

k7-rule2.text: This is the most common way to talk about plans. Use the present of *ir*, then *a*, then the infinitive.

k7-h3.text: estar + gerund: what is happening right now

head: Rule
Examples
cells: -ir verbs with a stem change: e → i, o → u

k7-m2.text: Spanish uses this for the moment of speaking, not for the future: *Mañana trabajo* or *Mañana voy a trabajar*, not *Mañana estoy trabajando*. With *ir* and *venir*, use the normal present: *¿Adónde vas?*

k7-err.text: After *hay que, tener que, poder, querer* and *ir a*, the second verb stays in the infinitive.

k8-intro.text: In Spain, two past tenses tell you what happened. The *pretérito perfecto* (*he comido*) is for time that is not finished. The *pretérito indefinido* (*comí*) is for finished time.

k8-rule1.text: The participle ends in *-ado* (*-ar* verbs) or *-ido* (*-er* and *-ir* verbs). It never changes, and nothing goes between it and *haber*: *No he comido.*

k8-m1.text: In Spain it goes with time words for time that is still going on, and with *ya, todavía no* and *nunca*: *Hoy he comido tarde. ¿Ya has pedido cita? Todavía no.* In much of Latin America people prefer the *indefinido* here: *Hoy comí tarde.*

k8-m2.text: The accent decides: *hablo* = I speak, *habló* = he or she spoke. Verbs in *-car, -gar, -zar* change their spelling with *yo*: *busqué, llegué, empecé*.

k8-m3.text: These irregular forms have no written accent: *tuve, hizo, fui*. *Ser* and *ir* share their forms; the sentence tells you which one it is: *Fue médica. Fue al médico.*

k8-rule2.text: When the time is finished (*ayer, el lunes, la semana pasada, en 2019, hace dos días*), use the *indefinido*. When the time is not finished or not mentioned, use the *perfecto*.

k8-err.text: *Ayer* is finished time, so in Spain you use the *indefinido*.

k9-intro.text: The *imperfecto* describes the past: what things were like, what was going on, what used to happen. Together with the *indefinido*, which says what happened next, it lets you tell a story.

k9-rule1.text: *-ar* verbs take *-aba*, and *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-ía*. The *yo* and *él* forms are the same. Only three verbs are irregular: *ser, ir* and *ver*.

head: Use
Example
cells: a habit, what used to happen
age, time and weather in the past
an action that was going on

k9-m1.text: *Antes* + *imperfecto* is the usual way to say “used to”: *Antes vivía en Rumanía; ahora vivo en Castellón.*

k9-rule2.text: Think of a film. The *imperfecto* is the background: the scene and the situation. The *indefinido* gives the events that move the story on.

k9-m2.text: A finished period with a clear length takes the *indefinido*: *Viví diez años en Rabat* (and then I left). Compare: *Vivía en Rabat cuando conocí a mi marido.*

k9-err.text: Your age in the past is background, so it takes the *imperfecto*.

k10-intro.text: This chapter brings together four things you need at B1: the *futuro*, the *condicional*, sentences with *si*, and your first steps with the *subjuntivo*. Each section shows the basic form; there is more practice online.

k10-rule1.text: Add the endings to the whole infinitive; all verbs have the same endings. Use it for predictions, promises and plans further away. For near plans, people usually say *ir a* + infinitive (Chapter 7).

k10-rule2.text: It has the same stems as the *futuro*, with the endings *-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían*: *hablaría, viviría, tendría, haría*. Use it to sound polite and to imagine something.

k10-rule3.text: *Si* + present, then a present, a future or an imperative. Use this for things that can really happen. When the *si* part comes first, put a comma after it.

k10-m1.text: There is no *futuro* and no present subjunctive right after *si*: *Si tengo tiempo, te llamaré*, not *Si tendré tiempo*. Imagined conditions (*Si tuviera…*) come at B2.

k10-rule4.text: Start from the *yo* form of the present and swap the vowel: *-ar* verbs take *e*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *a*: *hablo → hable, como → coma, tengo → tenga, hago → haga*.

head: When
Example
cells: a wish for someone else: quiero que, espero que
a future time: cuando, en cuanto, hasta que

k10-m2.text: Same person: infinitive. *Quiero ir.* Different person: *que* + subjunctive. *Quiero que vayas.* After *creo que*, use the normal present: *Creo que viene.* For a habit, *cuando* also takes the normal present: *Cuando llego a casa, cocino.*

k10-err.text: Right after *si*, use the present, even when you mean the future.
